newsitem.title: UK: SNOOKER 'GLADIATOR IN A SUIT' SHOWS AGE NO BARRIER.
newsitem.headline: SNOOKER 'GLADIATOR IN A SUIT' SHOWS AGE NO BARRIER.

text.p: With a conspicuous two-year absence from the winner's circle, six-time snooker world champion Steve Davis faced a fleet of brash young players and 28-1 odds against him at the Benson and Hedges Masters last weekend.
In the final, he found himself nearly hopelessly behind a charged-up and highly-skilled opponent 17 years his junior in Ronnie O' Sullivan.
But perhaps even more daunting, Davis faced a five-year-old son too young to remember his parent as a champion and convinced his father could never win.
With the candour of youth, Greg Davis had told his father: "You play, you lose, and someone else picks up the trophy."
"He thought that's what I did for a living," Davis explained. "But now he knows what it means to win."

The 39-year old veteran staged a masterful comeback and clawed his way from an 8-4 deficit to win 10-8 and in the process pocketed a career-high jackpot of 135,000 pounds ($220,000) -- plus a 15,000 pounds bonus for the highest tournament break.
"When it was all over, I was just in shock. I knew I had the chance and had the momentum, but I still had to get over the line," Davis said.

He compared his triumph to Jack Nicklaus's 1986 Masters victory in Augusta, Georgia. "This may well be my greatest performance ever," said the man who dominated professional snooker in the 1980s and has racked up 71 titles and won 4.5 million pounds in his prolific career.

Mild-mannered and renowned for his straightness, Davis reflected on the sport that has brought him so much and revealed the tiger within: "It is one of the cruellest and most aggressive games I know where the players never touch each other. You're going for the throat in exactly the same way boxers do."
"The fact that we're dressed up belies the aggression and the desires," he said. "We're really gladiators in dress suits."

That cut-throat atmosphere was partly defused during the Masters final last Sunday when a naked woman jumped out of the audience and streaked around the snooker table, and may well have given the composed Davis a psychological boost.
"She probably did me a big favour. She broke the spell of what was happening in the match and lightened things up a bit," he said, adding that he looked away so as not to break his concentration.
During his golden years in the 1980s when he won six world championships, Davis said the audience often seemed to want to see him lose.
"But this time it was different. The crowd seemed very much on my side. That was much more enjoyable than any win in the 80s," he said.
"A bit of failure does help you to appreciate something."
Davis again faces some of the world's top snooker players at the International in Aberdeen, Scotland this weekend, but sounded almost philosophical in his outlook.
"It doesn't matter now whether I win or lose," he said.
The Masters victory helped bolster his confidence and lift the pressure of being a has-been who seemed to have lost his magic touch.
"Whereas before I was searching for some form, desperate for a win on the table, I can now relax and that means I've got more chances of doing well," Davis explained.
"And that makes me more dangerous."
After so many years on the circuit that he took by storm as a young man, Davis has no intention of retiring.

"I sometimes think of (tennis player) Bjorn Borg, who must kick himself for retiring when he possibly wasn't finished. I'm not going to retire at the top because I want to get as much enjoyment out of the game as possible," he said.
"And I enjoy winning," Davis added.
When not hunched over the snooker table practising five to six hours a day or spending time with his family, Davis collects soul records and owns thousands of them.
Asked what his favourite one was, Davis paused briefly, then chuckled. "There's a good one called 'A Quitter Never Wins'," he said. "If you quit trying, you never have a chance."
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
